title: I built a free, open-source tool that turns AI-generated pixel-art-style images into usable game assets
author: HappyOnigiriJP
selftext:
AI image generators can make something that looks like pixel art at normal size, but the file often falls apart when you try to use it in a game: blurred anti-aliased edges, an inconsistent pixel grid, too many near-identical colors, and a background that is difficult to remove cleanly.



I built Pixel Refiner to automate that cleanup. The key step is estimating the repeated source-pixel cell size before resampling; a normal resize blends neighboring logical pixels and preserves the blur. When the grid estimate is uncertain, the tool exposes alternative candidates instead of silently committing to one result.



After grid correction, it can remove the background, trim transparent margins, reduce the palette, add dithering or outlines, and export scaled assets or a batch ZIP. Processing runs locally in the browser, so images are not uploaded.



The tool is free, requires no account, and the source is available under the MIT license.



Live app: [https://pixel-refiner.app/](https://pixel-refiner.app/)

Source: [https://github.com/HappyOnigiri/PixelRefiner](https://github.com/HappyOnigiri/PixelRefiner)



I made it because AI-generated sprites and icons can look convincing in a prompt result but still need a surprising amount of manual cleanup before they fit into an actual game pipeline. I’d be interested to hear which failure cases are still the most painful in your workflows.

replies.author: HappyOnigiriJP
replies.body:
Thanks! Pixel Refiner is hosted on Vercel’s free Hobby plan, so hosting costs me $0. The only expense is the \`.app\` domain, which I registered through Cloudflare Registrar for $14.20 per year.



Because all image processing happens locally in the browser, there are no server-side compute or image-storage costs. So at the moment, the entire service costs just $14.20 a year to keep online.

replies.author: HappyOnigiriJP
replies.body: Those are good options for ML-based pixelization, especially inside ComfyUI. Pixel Refiner is aimed at a different workflow: it runs locally in the browser with no setup or model downloads, and focuses on recovering the underlying grid of AI-generated “fake pixel art.” It also includes background removal, trimming, palette reduction, outlines, scaling, and batch export. There is some overlap, but the intended workflow and trade-offs are different.

replies.author: HappyOnigiriJP
replies.body:
Thanks for the suggestion. That project is mainly designed to turn conventional illustrations into pixel art, which is a different problem from the one Pixel Refiner is trying to solve.



AI-generated images that already look like pixel art often contain anti-aliased edges, inconsistent cell sizes, and grid drift. Converting those into clean, grid-aligned pixel art requires recovering the underlying logical pixel size first, and most existing pixelization tools aren’t built for that.



Before building Pixel Refiner, I tested PixelAid and pixeldetector, which do support pixel-art-style inputs. In my test cases, however, they often failed to identify the correct logical pixel size, so the reconstructed output still didn’t align to a consistent native pixel grid.



That gap is why I built Pixel Refiner. Its core is detecting the correct source-pixel cell size from blurred or anti-aliased AI-generated pixel-art-style images, then reconstructing them on a clean, consistent grid.



I’ve attached a comparison of the pixel-size detection results.

https://preview.redd.it/11s5alqirekh1.png?width=880&format=png&auto=webp&s=c7570e767e894a1835d2c0b676bd9031adbe62f2
